chapters.title: Section 1
paragraphs: Some things are within our control, others are not. Within our control are our opinions, impulses, desires, and aversions—what we seek to avoid. In short, whatever is our own doing. Outside our control are our body, reputation, possessions, and positions of power — in short, whatever is not our own doing. What is within our control is by nature free, unhindered, unobstructed. What is outside our control is weak, dependent, subject to obstruction — it belongs to others. Remember: if you mistake what is dependent for what is free, or what belongs to others for your own, you will be frustrated, you will grieve, you will be in turmoil, blaming gods and men alike. But if you take as your own only what truly is your own, and recognise that what belongs to others belongs to others, no one will ever compel you or obstruct you. You will blame no one, accuse no one, do nothing against your will. You will have no enemies, and nothing can harm you.

If you aim at such great things, remember that you cannot pursue them with a small effort. Some things must be given up entirely, and others set aside for now. But if you pursue this freedom alongside worldly power and wealth, you may fail to gain even the power and wealth because you are pursuing freedom too. You will certainly miss what alone can secure happiness and freedom. An impression is how something first appears to you. Practise saying at once to every disturbing impression: "You are only an impression, and not at all what you appear to be." Then examine it by the rules you possess, first and above all by asking whether it concerns something within our control or something outside it. If it concerns something outside our control, be ready to say: "This does not concern me."

chapters.title: Section 2
paragraphs: Remember: desire holds out the hope of obtaining what you desire, while aversion holds out the hope of avoiding what you try to escape. Whoever fails to get what they desire is unfortunate; whoever falls into what they try to avoid is unhappy. If you try to avoid only what is contrary to nature among the things within your control, you will not fall into anything you seek to avoid. But if you try to avoid illness, death, or poverty, you will be unhappy. Remove aversion, then, from everything outside your control, and direct it toward what is contrary to nature within your control. For the present, give up desire entirely. If you desire anything outside your control, you are bound to be unfortunate; and of the good things within your control, nothing is yet before you to desire. Use only your impulses to move toward or away from things, and use even these gently, with reservation, and without strain.

chapters.title: Section 3
paragraphs: With anything that pleases you, meets a need, or is dear to you, remind yourself what it is. Start with small things. If you love a clay cup, say to yourself: it is a clay cup that I love. When it breaks, you will not be disturbed. If you kiss your child or your wife, say: it is a human being I am kissing. When they die, you will not be disturbed.

chapters.title: Section 4
paragraphs: Before taking on any activity, picture what it involves. If you are going to the baths, picture what happens there—people splashing, jostling, insulting one another, and stealing. Then you will undertake it more safely if you say to yourself: "I intend to bathe, and I also intend to keep my will in accordance with nature." Do this with every activity. That way, if something prevents you from bathing, you can say: "Bathing was not my only intention. I also intended to keep my will in accordance with nature, and I will not do that if I am upset by what happens."

chapters.title: Section 5
paragraphs: People are not disturbed by events but by their opinions about events. Death, for instance, is nothing terrible — if it were, it would have seemed terrible to Socrates. What is terrible is the opinion that death is terrible. So whenever we are frustrated, troubled, or distressed, let us never blame others, but ourselves — meaning our own opinions. It is the sign of an untrained person to blame others for their troubles; of one beginning to learn, to blame themselves; of one whose learning is complete, to blame neither others nor themselves.

chapters.title: Section 6
paragraphs: Do not take pride in advantages that belong to someone else. If a horse could say proudly "I am beautiful," that would be tolerable. But when you say proudly "I have a beautiful horse," you should know that you are taking pride in something that belongs to the horse. What is actually yours? How you judge and respond to your impressions. When you do this in accordance with nature, then be proud — for then you are proud of something genuinely good, and genuinely yours.

chapters.title: Section 7
paragraphs: On a sea voyage, when the ship reaches a port and you go ashore for water, you may amuse yourself by picking up a shellfish or a plant bulb along the way. But keep your thoughts on the ship and watch constantly for the captain's call. When he calls, throw everything aside, so that you are not tied up and thrown aboard like sheep. Life is like this too. If you are given a wife and child instead of a little bulb and a shell, there is nothing to prevent you from accepting them. But when the captain calls, run to the ship and leave everything without a second thought. If you are old, do not even go far from the ship, or you may fail to return when called.

chapters.title: Section 8
paragraphs: Do not demand that events happen as you wish. Wish them to happen as they do, and your life will flow peacefully.

chapters.title: Section 9
paragraphs: Illness is an obstacle to the body, but not to the will, unless the will consents to it. A disability is an obstacle to the leg, but not to the will. Apply this reflection to everything that happens to you: you will find it is an obstacle to something, but not to you.

chapters.title: Section 10
paragraphs: Whenever an event befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and ask what capacity you have to make use of it. If you see an attractive man or woman, you will find in yourself the capacity for self-restraint. If you face hard work or pain, you will find endurance. If you face abusive words, you will find patience. Once you have formed this habit, impressions will not sweep you away.

chapters.title: Section 11
paragraphs: Never say about anything "I have lost it," but say "I have returned it." Is your child dead? They have been returned. Is your wife dead? She has been returned. Has your property been taken? That too has been returned. "But the one who took it is a bad person." What does it matter to you who the giver used to reclaim it? While you have it, treat it as a traveller treats an inn — care for it, but as something that belongs to another.

chapters.title: Section 12
paragraphs: If you are working to improve yourself, let go of thoughts like: "If I neglect my affairs, I will have nothing to live on," or "Unless I discipline my slave, he will behave badly." It is better to die of hunger free from grief and fear than to live in abundance troubled and anxious. And it is better for your slave to behave badly than for you to be unhappy. Begin with small things. Has some oil been spilled? Has a little wine been stolen? Say: "This is the price of freedom from distress; this is the price of peace of mind. Nothing comes for nothing." When you call your slave, bear in mind that he may not hear; and if he does hear, he may do nothing you want. He is not the one in such a fortunate position; you are. Your freedom from distress must not lie in his power.

chapters.title: Section 13
paragraphs: If you want to improve, be willing to be thought foolish and ignorant about things outside your control. Wish to appear to know nothing. And if you start to seem important in anyone's eyes, distrust yourself. Because it is not easy to both keep your will aligned with nature and pursue things outside your control — whoever is careful about one will necessarily neglect the other.

chapters.title: Section 14
paragraphs: To wish your children, wife, and friends to live forever is foolish: you are wishing for things outside your control to be in your control, and for what belongs to others to be yours. Likewise, if you wish your slave to be free from faults, you are foolish; you are wishing badness not to be badness, but something else. But if you wish not to fail in your desires, that is within your power. Practise, then, what you are able to do. Anyone who controls the things another person wants or seeks to avoid—who can grant or take them away—is that person's master. Whoever wants to be free must neither desire nor avoid anything that depends on others. Otherwise, that person must be a slave.

chapters.title: Section 15
paragraphs: Remember to behave in life as you would at a banquet. When a dish is passed to you, reach out and take your portion gracefully. When it passes by, don't hold it back. When it hasn't reached you yet, do not long for it ahead of time—wait until it comes to you. Do this with children, with a spouse, with public office, with wealth, and you will prove a worthy guest at the gods' own table. But if you don't even take what is offered, even look down on it — then you will share not just the gods' banquet but their power. This is how Diogenes and Heraclitus and those like them deserved to be called divine, and were.

chapters.title: Section 16
paragraphs: When you see someone weeping in grief — because a child has gone away, or died, or because they have lost property — be careful not to be carried away by the appearance that they are suffering from external events. Draw a distinction in your own mind and be ready to say: what distresses this person is not what has happened — the same thing would not distress someone else — but their opinion about what has happened. In your words, by all means sympathise with them and even mourn aloud with them if the moment calls for it. But do not grieve inside as well.

chapters.title: Section 17
paragraphs: Remember that you are an actor in a play of whatever kind its author chooses. If he wants it short, it is short; if long, long. If he wants you to play a poor man, play that role naturally; if someone with a disabled leg, a magistrate, an ordinary person — do the same. Your duty is to act well the part you have been given. But choosing the part belongs to someone else.

chapters.title: Section 18
paragraphs: When a raven croaks ominously, do not be carried away by the impression. Immediately draw this distinction: none of these signs concerns me, but only my poor body, my small property, my reputation, my children, or my wife. For me, every omen can be a good sign if I choose, because whatever happens, it is within my power to benefit from it.

chapters.title: Section 19
paragraphs: You can be undefeatable if you never enter a contest where victory is not within your power. When you see someone honoured, powerful, or highly regarded, be careful not to assume they are happy — don't be swept away by appearances. If what is good lies within our power, there is no place for envy or jealousy. You will not wish to be a general, a senator, a consul — you will wish to be free. And there is only one road to freedom: not caring about things outside your power.

chapters.title: Section 20
paragraphs: Remember that it is not the person who insults or strikes you who humiliates you, but your own opinion about what they have done. When someone angers you, know that it is your own judgment that has angered you. Most importantly: try not to be swept away in the moment. If you gain even a little time and pause, you will find it far easier to master yourself.

chapters.title: Section 21
paragraphs: Keep death before your eyes every day, along with exile and everything else that seems dreadful—but death above all. Then you will never think anything dishonourable or desire anything excessive.

chapters.title: Section 22
paragraphs: If you commit yourself to philosophy, prepare from the start to be laughed at. Expect many people to sneer and say: "He has suddenly come back to us as a philosopher. Where did he get that superior look?" Do not look superior. Hold fast to what seems best to you, as someone appointed by God to this post. Remember that if you remain true to the same principles, those who first ridiculed you will later admire you. But if they overpower you, you will bring double ridicule on yourself.

chapters.title: Section 23
paragraphs: If you ever find yourself turning toward things outside your control in order to please someone, know that you have lost your purpose. Be content to be a philosopher in everything. If you want anyone to see you as a philosopher, let that person be yourself. This is within your power.

chapters.title: Section 24
paragraphs: Do not let thoughts like these trouble you: "I will live without honour and be nobody anywhere." If lack of honor is an evil, another person can no more involve you in evil than in anything shameful. Is it your business to gain public office or be invited to a banquet? Not at all. How, then, can missing these things be dishonor? And how can you be nobody anywhere, when you need to be somebody only in the things within your power, where you are free to be a person of the greatest worth? "But my friends will go without help!" What do you mean by "without help"? They will not receive money from you, and you will not make them Roman citizens. Who told you that these things are within our power rather than someone else's? And who can give another what he does not have himself? "Then acquire money," your friends say, "so that we may have something too." If I can acquire money while remaining modest, faithful, and generous in spirit, show me the way and I will acquire it. But if you ask me to lose the good things that are truly mine so that you may gain things that are not good, see how unfair and foolish you are. Besides, which would you rather have: money, or a faithful and modest friend? Help me, then, to become such a person, and do not ask me to act in a way that would make me lose that character. "But my country, as far as it depends on me, will go without my help." Again I ask, what help do you mean? It will not get covered walkways lined with columns or public baths from you. What of it? A blacksmith does not provide it with shoes, nor a shoemaker with weapons. It is enough if everyone fully performs their own work. If you provided your country with one more faithful and modest citizen, would you not be useful to it? Yes. Then you cannot be useless to it either. "What position, then, will I hold in the city?" Whatever position you can hold while preserving your faithfulness and modesty. But if, in trying to be useful to the state, you lose these qualities, what use could you be to it once you had become shameless and unfaithful?

chapters.title: Section 25
paragraphs: Has someone else been preferred over you at a banquet, in being greeted, or in being invited to give advice? If these things are good, you should be glad that person received them; if they are bad, do not be upset that you did not. Remember that if you do not do the same things others do to obtain what lies outside our control, you cannot expect an equal share. How can someone who does not visit a powerful person's door, accompany him when he goes out, or flatter him receive the same treatment as someone who does? You are unfair and insatiable if you refuse to pay the price for which these things are sold but still want to receive them for nothing. What is the price of lettuces? An obolus—a small coin—perhaps. Someone pays the coin and gets the lettuces. You do not pay it and do not get them. Do not think that you have less: that person has the lettuces, and you still have the coin you did not pay. The same is true here. You were not invited to a person's dinner because you did not pay the host's price: he sells it for flattery and personal attention. Pay that price, if doing so is in your interest. But if you want both to avoid paying and to receive the goods, you are insatiable and foolish. Have you received nothing in place of the dinner? You have: you did not flatter the person you chose not to flatter, and you did not have to endure him when he entered the room.

chapters.title: Section 26
paragraphs: We can learn what nature wants from the things on which we all agree. When your neighbour's slave breaks a cup, you say straightaway: "These things happen." You must know that when your own cup breaks, you should think the same. Apply this to larger things too. When someone else's child or wife dies, anyone would say: "That is something that happens to people." But when your own child or wife dies, you cry out: "What a disaster, how wretched I am!" Remember how you felt when you heard it happen to someone else.

chapters.title: Section 27
paragraphs: A target is not set up in order to be missed. In the same way, evil does not naturally exist in the world.

chapters.title: Section 28
paragraphs: If someone intended to put your body in the power of any stranger you met on the road, you would be upset. Yet you put your mind in the power of anyone you meet, letting it become disturbed and troubled if they insult you. Are you not ashamed of that?

chapters.title: Section 29
paragraphs: Before you act, consider what must come first and what will follow. Then proceed. Otherwise you will begin eagerly, without thinking about what comes next, and later feel ashamed when unpleasant things appear. Someone wants to win at the Olympic Games. So do I—it is a fine thing. But consider both what comes first and what follows, and only then begin. You must follow a strict routine, eat as instructed, give up delicacies, and train at set times as you are told, in heat and cold. You must not drink cold water or drink wine whenever you like. In short, you must put yourself in your trainer's hands as you would in a doctor's, and then enter the contest. Sometimes you will strain your hand, dislocate your ankle, swallow a great deal of dust, or be flogged—and after all this, lose. Once you have considered everything, enter the contest if you still choose to. If you do not consider it, you will behave like children who play at being wrestlers, then flute players, then gladiators, trumpeters, and tragic actors. You too will be an athlete one moment, a gladiator the next, then a teacher of public speaking, then a philosopher, but you will be nothing with your whole soul. Like an ape, you imitate everything you see, and one thing after another pleases you. You have not thought carefully about what you are taking on or examined it closely; you have approached it carelessly, with only half-hearted desire. Some people see a philosopher and hear someone speak as Euphrates does—and who can speak like him?—and want to become philosophers themselves. My friend, first consider what this involves, then examine your own nature to see whether you can live up to the role. Do you want to compete in the pentathlon—the five-event contest—or to wrestle? Look at your arms, your thighs, and your lower back. Different people are naturally suited to different things. Do you think you can take this on and still eat, drink, and dislike things just as before? You must go without sleep, endure hard work, leave your family, be despised by a slave, and take the lower place in everything: honours, public office, the law courts, every little matter. Consider whether you are willing to accept these things in exchange for freedom from passions, liberty, and peace of mind. If not, take care not to be like a little child: a philosopher now, then an assistant to tax collectors, then a teacher of public speaking, then a manager for Caesar. These roles do not fit together. You must be one person, either good or bad. You must cultivate either your ruling mind—the part that judges and chooses—or things outside you. You must work on what is within you or on what is outside you: in other words, live as a philosopher or as an ordinary person.

chapters.title: Section 30
paragraphs: Our duties are always measured by our relationships. Is someone your father? Your duty is to care for him, yield to him in everything, and submit when he insults or beats you. But suppose he is a bad father. Did nature make you the child of a good father? No, of a father. Does your brother wrong you? Keep to your own part in that relationship. Do not examine what he is doing, but what you must do to keep your will in accordance with nature. Another person will not harm you unless you choose it: you are harmed when you think you are harmed. In this way you will discover your duty as a neighbour, a citizen, or a general, if you make a habit of considering your relationships.

chapters.title: Section 31
paragraphs: In devotion to the gods, the most important thing is to hold right opinions about them: that they exist and govern the universe well and justly. Commit yourself to obeying them, accepting everything that happens, and following it willingly as the work of the wisest intelligence. If you do this, you will never blame the gods or accuse them of neglecting you. There is no way to do this except by turning away from what is outside our control and placing good and evil only in what is within our control. If you count anything outside our control as good or bad, then whenever you fail to get what you want or encounter what you want to avoid, you will inevitably blame and hate those responsible. Every living creature is naturally inclined to flee and turn away from what seems harmful and whatever causes that harm, and to pursue and admire what is useful and whatever brings it about. Someone who believes they have been harmed cannot take pleasure in what they believe caused the harm, any more than in the harm itself. This is also why a son curses his father when his father gives him no share of what people consider good. The belief that royal power was good made Polynices and Eteocles enemies. It is why farmers, sailors, and merchants curse the gods, and why people who lose their wives and children do so. Where your interest lies, there your devotion lies too. Whoever takes care to desire and avoid as they ought also takes care of their devotion to the gods. But everyone should pour ritual drink offerings, make sacrifices, and offer the first fruits of the harvest according to the customs of our ancestors. Do this with purity, neither grudgingly nor carelessly, neither stingily nor beyond your means.

chapters.title: Section 32
paragraphs: When you turn to divination—seeking signs of the future—remember that you do not know how things will turn out. That is what you have come to ask the diviner. But if you are a philosopher, you already know what kind of thing the outcome is: if it lies outside our control, it must be neither good nor bad. Do not bring desire or aversion to the diviner, or you will approach in fear. Instead, settle in your mind that whatever happens is neither good nor bad and does not concern you. Whatever it is, you can use it well, and no one can prevent that. Then come confidently to the gods as your advisers. Once they have given advice, remember whom you chose as advisers and whom you will have disregarded if you do not obey. As Socrates said, consult divination about questions that turn entirely on the outcome, where neither reasoning nor any skill gives you a way to find the answer. So when you ought to share a friend's danger, or your country's, do not ask a diviner whether you should. Even if the diviner says the signs in the sacrificial animals are unfavourable, clearly pointing to death, the loss of a body part, or exile, reason still requires us to share the dangers of our friends and country despite those risks. Listen, then, to the greater diviner, the god at Delphi, who drove from his temple the man who failed to help his friend while that friend was being murdered.

chapters.title: Section 33
paragraphs: Set yourself a character and a way of behaving now, and keep to them both when you are alone and when you meet others.

As a rule, be silent, or say only what is needed, in few words. Speak rarely, when the occasion calls for it, but not about the usual subjects: gladiators, horse races, athletes, food or drink. Above all, do not talk about people to blame or praise them, or to compare them. If you can, steer your companions' conversation towards what is proper. But if you find yourself stuck in the company of strangers, stay silent.
Do not laugh much, often, or excessively.
Refuse to take oaths altogether if you can; if not, refuse as far as you are able.

Avoid banquets given by strangers and people untrained in philosophy. If you have occasion to attend, watch yourself carefully so that you do not slip into their ways. You must know that if your companion is morally unclean, keeping their company will make you unclean too, even if you are clean yourself.
Use things for the body only to meet basic needs: food, drink, clothing, housing, and slaves. Leave out everything intended for show or luxury.

As for sex with women, abstain as far as you can before marriage. If you do indulge, keep to accepted custom. But do not be unpleasant to those who indulge or scold them, and do not often boast that you abstain yourself.
If someone tells you that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not defend yourself against the report. Reply: "He did not know my other faults, or he would not have mentioned only these."

You do not need to go to the theatre often. If there is a proper occasion to go, do not take anyone's side except your own: want only what happens to happen, and only the person who wins to win. In this way you will meet with no obstacle. Abstain entirely from shouting, laughing at anything or anyone, and violent emotion. Afterwards, do not talk much about what happened on stage, except what might help you improve. If you talk a great deal about it, you plainly admired the spectacle more than you should.
Do not readily go to hear people recite or visit them. If you do attend, be serious and composed, but avoid making yourself unpleasant.

When you are going to meet someone, especially a person considered above you in rank, picture what Socrates or Zeno would have done in those circumstances. You will have no difficulty making proper use of the occasion.

When you go to visit someone very powerful, picture finding him away from home, being refused entry, finding the door closed to you, or meeting with his indifference. If, despite all this, it is your duty to visit, bear what happens. Never tell yourself it was not worth the trouble. That is foolish, and shows someone upset by things outside their control.

In company, take care not to talk too much about your own deeds or dangers. Recalling your dangers may please you, but hearing what happened to you is not as pleasant for others. Be careful, too, not to try to make people laugh. It is an easy way to slip into vulgar habits and lose your neighbours' respect. Drifting into obscene talk is dangerous as well. If this happens and there is a good opening, rebuke the person who began it. If not, show your displeasure plainly at least through silence, a blush, and your expression.

chapters.title: Section 34
paragraphs: When the thought of a pleasure strikes you, guard against being swept away by it. Let it wait; give yourself a little time. Think of both moments: when you will enjoy the pleasure, and afterwards, when you will regret it and reproach yourself. Weigh against these the joy and self-approval you will feel if you abstain. But if you think the time is right to act, take care not to be overcome by its charm, pleasure, and attraction. Set against them how much better it is to know that you have won this victory.

chapters.title: Section 35
paragraphs: When you have decided that something ought to be done and are doing it, never avoid being seen, even if most people disapprove. If it is wrong, avoid doing it. But if it is right, why fear those who wrongly find fault?

chapters.title: Section 36
paragraphs: In logic, "It is day or it is night" works as an either-or statement, but not as a both-and statement. In the same way, taking the larger share at a dinner serves your body well but does nothing to preserve good relations with others. When you eat with someone, consider not only what the food offers your body, but also the value of behaving as you should towards your host.

chapters.title: Section 37
paragraphs: If you take on a role beyond your strength, you both perform it badly and neglect the role you could have fulfilled.

chapters.title: Section 38
paragraphs: When walking, you take care not to step on a nail or sprain your foot. Take the same care not to damage your ruling mind. If we follow this rule in every action, we will act more safely.

chapters.title: Section 39
paragraphs: Your body sets the measure of your possessions, just as your foot sets the measure of your shoe. Keep to what the body needs, and you will keep to the right measure. Go beyond it, and you will inevitably be swept along as if down a cliff. With shoes, once you go beyond what the foot needs, the shoe is gilded, then dyed purple, then embroidered. Once the proper limit is passed, there is no end.

chapters.title: Section 40
paragraphs: As soon as girls reach fourteen, men address them as "mistresses"—ladies. Seeing that they can gain nothing else but the power to sleep with men, they begin to adorn themselves and place all their hopes in that. We should take care, then, that they know men value them only for being decent, modest, and sensible.

chapters.title: Section 41
paragraphs: It is a sign of a limited mind to spend much time on bodily matters: too much exercise, eating, drinking, relieving yourself, or sex. These should be secondary concerns. Direct all your care towards the mind.

chapters.title: Section 42
paragraphs: When someone treats you badly or speaks ill of you, remember that they act or speak because they think it is their duty. They cannot follow what seems right to you, only what seems right to them. If their judgment is wrong, they are the one harmed, because they are mistaken. If someone thinks a true combined statement—claims joined by "and"—is false, the statement is not harmed; the person mistaken about it is. Keep this in mind and you will be gentle with anyone who insults you. Say each time: "That is how it seemed to them."

chapters.title: Section 43
paragraphs: Everything has two handles: one by which it can be carried, and one by which it cannot. If your brother acts unjustly, do not grasp the matter by his injustice—that handle will not bear it. Grasp the other handle: he is your brother, and you were brought up together. Then you will have a handle by which you can carry it.

chapters.title: Section 44
paragraphs: These arguments do not follow: "I am richer than you, so I am better than you"; "I speak more eloquently than you, so I am better than you." These, however, do follow: "I am richer than you, so my possessions are greater than yours"; "I speak more eloquently than you, so my speech is better than yours." But you are neither your possessions nor your speech.

chapters.title: Section 45
paragraphs: Does someone bathe quickly? Do not say they bathe badly; say they bathe quickly. Does someone drink a lot of wine? Do not say they do it badly; say they drink a lot. Until you have established the judgment behind their action, how do you know whether they are doing wrong? In this way, you will not take in one set of impressions as facts and then accept a different set as true.

chapters.title: Section 46
paragraphs: Never call yourself a philosopher, and do not talk much about philosophical principles among people untrained in philosophy. Act on those principles instead. At a banquet, for example, do not explain how people ought to eat; eat as you ought. Remember how completely Socrates avoided showing off. People would come to him and ask him to recommend philosophers, and he would take them to philosophers, so readily did he accept being overlooked. If a conversation about a philosophical principle arises among people untrained in philosophy, generally stay silent. There is a great danger that you will immediately vomit up what you have not digested. When someone tells you that you know nothing and you are not upset, be sure that you have begun the work of philosophy. Even sheep do not vomit up their grass to show the shepherds how much they have eaten. They digest their food within and produce wool and milk outside. In the same way, do not display your principles to people untrained in philosophy. Show the actions that come from digesting them.

chapters.title: Section 47
paragraphs: When you can meet all your body's needs at little cost, do not be proud of it. If you drink water, do not announce at every opportunity, "I drink water." First consider how much more frugally the poor live than we do, and how much more hard work they endure. If you want to train yourself in hard work and endurance, do it for yourself, not for others. Do not embrace statues. If you are very thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one.

chapters.title: Section 48
paragraphs: Someone untrained in philosophy never expects benefit or harm to come from themselves, but from things outside them. A philosopher expects all benefit and harm to come from themselves. These are the signs of someone making progress: they criticise no one, praise no one, blame no one, and accuse no one. They say nothing about themselves as though they were important or knew something. When obstructed or hindered, they blame themselves. If someone praises them, they privately laugh at the person praising them; if someone criticises them, they make no defence. They move about like someone physically weak, careful not to disturb anything that has been put in place before it is firmly settled. They set aside all desire and direct aversion only towards what is contrary to nature among the things within our control. Their impulses towards everything are moderate. They do not care whether others consider them foolish or ignorant. In short, they watch themselves as though they were an enemy lying in ambush.

chapters.title: Section 49
paragraphs: When someone is proud of understanding and explaining Chrysippus's writings, say to yourself: "If Chrysippus had not written so obscurely, this person would have nothing to be proud of." What do I want? To understand nature and follow it. So I ask who can explain it, and when I hear that Chrysippus can, I turn to him. But I do not understand what he has written, so I seek someone to explain it. So far there is nothing to be proud of. Once I have found an interpreter, what remains is to put the lessons into practice. That alone is something to be proud of. If I merely admire the explanation, what have I become but a scholar of texts instead of a philosopher? The only difference is that I explain Chrysippus rather than Homer. So when someone asks me to read Chrysippus to them, I feel ashamed if I cannot show actions that agree with his words.

chapters.title: Section 50
paragraphs: Hold to the rules laid down for your conduct as if they were laws, and breaking any of them would violate a sacred duty. Pay no attention to what anyone says about you; it is not your concern. How much longer will you put off considering yourself worthy of the best things and never acting against the reason that distinguishes you? Have you accepted the principles you ought to accept, and agreed to them? What teacher are you still waiting for, leaving your own correction until they arrive? You are no longer a youth but a grown adult. If you remain careless and lazy, postponing again and again, making plan after plan and setting date after date to begin attending to yourself, you will not notice that you are making no progress. You will remain untrained throughout your life and at your death. Decide now to live as a grown adult who is making progress. Treat whatever seems best to you as a law you must not break. If anything hard or pleasant, glorious or shameful, comes your way, remember: the contest is now, the Olympic Games are now, and they cannot be postponed. A single defeat, a single surrender, determines whether your progress is lost or maintained. This is how Socrates became perfect: improving himself in everything and attending to nothing but reason. Though you are not yet Socrates, live as someone who wishes to be like him.

chapters.title: Section 51
paragraphs: The first and most necessary part of philosophy is putting principles into practice: for example, that we must not lie. The second is proving those principles: how do we prove that we ought not to lie? The third supports and explains the first two: how does this count as a proof? What is a proof? What follows logically from something else? What is a contradiction? What is truth, and what is falsehood? The third part is needed for the second, and the second for the first. But the first is the most necessary, and the one we should concentrate on. We do the opposite. We spend our time and all our effort on the third part, while entirely neglecting the first. So we lie, but have the proof that we ought not to lie ready to hand.

chapters.title: Section 52
paragraphs: In every situation, keep these sayings ready:

Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny,
Along the path you bid me take.
I am ready to follow. If I refuse,
I make myself miserable—and still must follow.

Whoever nobly yields to necessity
We call wise, and skilled in divine things.
And this third saying too: "Crito, if this pleases the gods, let it be. Anytus and Melitus can indeed kill me, but they cannot harm me."
